pedagogy.summary: This topic teaches children to read rock layers (strata) as a record of time: layers are deposited over long periods with the oldest at the bottom (superposition), and fossils in different layers are evidence of organisms that lived at different times, so patterns in rock formations reveal how a landscape changed over millions of years. It is best taught with a built-up sediment model and real strata (e.g. the Grand Canyon), keeping to RELATIVE ordering of events rather than absolute dates or the detailed mechanism of rock formation.
bestPractices: Build superposition physically — lay down sediment layers over 'time' and bury objects/organisms in each — so the oldest-at-the-bottom rule is constructed, not asserted.
Use fossils as time-markers: different fossils in different layers show different organisms lived at different times; the order of layers gives the order of events.
Keep to RELATIVE time (which is older/younger, what happened before what), not absolute dates — matching the assessment boundary.
Read real, dramatic strata (canyon walls, cliff faces) so pupils apply the rule to genuine evidence of landscape change.
Have pupils construct an explanation of how a landscape changed over time FROM the pattern of layers and fossils, rather than being told the story.
Use correct vocabulary (sediment, strata, fossil, layer) established in the linked rocks topic, but keep the focus on the ordering inference.
keyRepresentations: A labelled strata cross-section with the oldest layer at the bottom.
A build-up-the-layers model (deposit sediment over time, bury an organism in each).
A fossil-in-layer timeline linking each fossil to its relative position/age.
A real canyon or cliff cutaway showing many layers.
commonMisconceptions: All rock layers formed at the same time, or the order of layers does not indicate time.
The youngest/oldest layer is at the top (reversing superposition).
Fossils are only dinosaur bones, or are just 'pictures in rocks', rather than remains of once-living organisms.
You can read the exact age of a layer directly by looking at it (confusing relative with absolute dating).
Landscapes are fixed — rather than the product of change recorded in the layers.

learn.summary: Children learn to read rock strata as a record of time: layers build up with the oldest at the bottom (superposition, which holds for layers that have not been folded, overturned or otherwise disturbed), and fossils in different layers are evidence of organisms that lived at different times, so patterns in the rock reveal how a landscape changed over long periods. The focus is the evidence-reading inference — ordering events and reconstructing landscape change from layers and fossils — kept to RELATIVE time (older/younger, before/after), never absolute dates or the detailed mechanism of rock formation.

activities.title: Build-up-the-layers time machine
feedback: If a learner orders the higher fossil as the earlier animal — e.g. reasoning 'it's been up there longest' — replay the build-up: each new layer lands ON TOP of the previous one, so the bottom layer formed first. Being higher means it arrived later, not earlier; oldest at the bottom, youngest at the top.
If a learner says all the layers and fossils formed together, emphasise that layers accumulate one atop another over long stretches of time, so different layers record different times.
Confirm correct reasoning by connecting a fossil's position to WHEN its organism lived: a lower fossil was buried longer ago, therefore that organism lived earlier.
Prompt for landscape change: a sea-creature fossil high on land shows that place was once underwater — so landscapes are not fixed but change over long time.
activities.rationale: The learning goal is an evidence-reading inference, which is served by having the child construct the layer order and perform the ordering reasoning rather than being told the story. Building superposition physically (laying sediment, burying organisms) makes the oldest-at-bottom rule something constructed and presents the common reversal and single-event misconceptions for correction.

Students commonly reverse superposition (thinking oldest is on top) and think fossils are only dinosaur bones; teaching the ordering with a build-up model addresses this.
learnerActions: Deposit sediment one layer at a time as 'time' passes, so each new layer settles on top of the last.
In each era, place/bury an organism in the layer being formed at that time (e.g. a trilobite early, an ammonite later).
Relate the build-up to a jar: pour in sand, then mud, then gravel, letting each settle before adding the next — the first poured ends up at the bottom, mirroring how the oldest layer sits lowest.
Cut into the resulting cliff/cross-section and read it back: order the buried fossils from earliest-lived to latest-lived.
State, in your own words, why the fossil in the lower layer must be older than the one above it.
Reconstruct how the landscape changed over time from the sequence of layers and the fossils in them.
activities.intendedInsight: The trilobite resting at the BOTTOM must be older than the ammonite above it, because its layer was deposited — and the organism buried — first. Undisturbed rock layers are a stack of time with the oldest underneath, so a landscape's history can be read from its layers.

activities.title: Read real strata and reconstruct the story
feedback: If the learner cannot connect a fossil's position to when its organism lived, point back to the build-up model: lower layer = buried earlier = organism lived earlier.
Reinforce landscape-change reasoning: ask what a sea fossil high on a hill tells you about that place long ago.
Keep answers to relative order (which came before which); if the learner reaches for exact ages, redirect — you cannot read an exact age off a layer just by looking at it.
activities.rationale: Applying the rule to real, dramatic strata lets pupils use the inference on authentic evidence and construct the explanation themselves, which is the stated objective. Transfer to a new cliff checks the ordering skill rather than recall of one example.

learnerActions: Examine a real, dramatic strata cross-section (a canyon wall or cliff face) with many visible layers that are flat-lying and not folded or overturned.
Identify which layers are older and younger using the oldest-at-the-bottom rule.
Match named fossils to the layers they appear in and order the organisms by relative time.
Write or say a short explanation of how this landscape changed over a long time, citing the layer/fossil pattern as evidence.
Transfer the reasoning to a second, unfamiliar cliff with undisturbed layers to check you can apply the rule to new evidence.
activities.intendedInsight: The ordering rule applies to genuine evidence: real rock formations whose layers have not been overturned record a sequence of events, and you can construct the landscape's history from the pattern of layers and fossils rather than memorising a told story.

activities.title: Labelled strata cross-section reference
feedback: Use this as a support when a learner is unsure of a term; then return them to building or reading a cliff so they perform the ordering themselves.

Correct 'fossils are only dinosaur bones' or 'just pictures in rock' — a fossil is the preserved remains or traces (such as imprints or footprints) of a once-living organism, from shells and plants as well as animals (often, over long time, the remains are gradually replaced by minerals; the full formation mechanism is covered in the linked prerequisite topic, so keep it brief here).
activities.rationale: A fixed, labelled reference consolidates vocabulary and the relative-age mapping. It is a scaffold: it displays the ordering rather than requiring the child to construct it, so it should accompany, not replace, the build-and-read activities.
learnerActions: Study a labelled strata cross-section with the oldest layer at the bottom.
Reveal, for a selected layer or fossil, its relative age and which organism it represents (e.g. tap or lift a panel).
Use it to check vocabulary: sediment, strata, fossil, layer.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear reference links each layer and fossil to its relative position and age, anchoring the vocabulary used when reasoning about order.

activities.title: Sequence and match check
feedback: If the higher fossil is picked as the earlier animal, this signals inverted superposition — revisit the build-up (new layers land on top, so the bottom is oldest).
If both animals are said to have lived at the same time, revisit that layers accumulate over long stretches of time, so different layers record different times.
A correct order can be selected without the underlying reason, so always pair the sequence with a 'how do you know?' to elicit and check the rule independently.
activities.rationale: Sequencing and matching are a natural fit for checking the ordering inference and surfacing the specific misconceptions. Requiring an explanation guards against a correct selection masking faulty reasoning; note that ordering well is evidence of the inference only when the reason is also produced.
sourceClaims: Students commonly reverse superposition (thinking oldest is on top) and think fossils are only dinosaur bones; teaching the ordering with a build-up model addresses this.
learnerActions: Order a set of layers from oldest to youngest.
Match each named fossil to the layer it belongs in.
Answer a short reasoning question on superposition, e.g. which of two fossils lived earlier and why.
Explain WHY, not just WHICH, so the rule you are using is visible.
activities.intendedInsight: Ordering and matching reveal whether the learner is applying superposition correctly and connecting fossil position to time, or using an inverted/single-event rule.

constraints: Keep to RELATIVE time (older/younger, before/after); do not teach absolute dates. You cannot read an exact age off a layer just by looking at it.

Do not teach the detailed mechanism of rock formation or require memorising specific layer names, per the assessment boundary. (Year 3 linked work covers that fossils form when once-living things are trapped in rock — use it only to correct the 'fossils are just pictures/only dinosaur bones' idea, without making mechanism the focus here.)
A fixed labelled cross-section is a scaffold: it shows the order but does not require the child to construct or infer it, so pair it with building/reading activities rather than using it alone.
A sequence or matching task can be completed by selection without the underlying reasoning; require a 'how do you know?' to elicit the rule being used.
A fly-through 3D canyon can convey scale and atmosphere, but the ordering/reading skill is fully served in a 2D cross-section; treat immersive 3D as optional enrichment, not a requirement.
Interviewing or listening to a character (e.g. a palaeontologist) can add context, but the ordering inference is better performed by the child than narrated to them.
Use correct vocabulary (sediment, strata, fossil, layer) but keep the focus on the ordering inference, not terminology drill.
Optional interaction examples (scrubbable time, dragging fossils into order, tap/lift-to-reveal panels) make the mechanism concrete but are not mandatory.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The DfE Year 3 'Rocks' claim and the general Earth-science misconceptions claim (including its assertion that a build-up model 'addresses' the reversal) were marked verified:false in the source; treat as unconfirmed, and read any efficacy wording as proposed/intended rather than demonstrated.

Self-audit of science logic: superposition (oldest at bottom, youngest on top) and reading fossil position as a record of relative time are internally consistent as stated across all activities; no superposition reversal or same-age slips remain. The jar analogy is framed as dry sequential pouring so first-poured sits lowest, avoiding density-settling confusion.

The reteach for the 'fossil = unchanged real bones' misconception concerns how fossils form (mineral replacement), which sits at the edge of this topic's relative-time boundary; it is kept light and deferred to the linked fossil-formation prerequisite topic.

The original 'moment of insight', the jar and sea-fossil-high-on-land examples, and the misconception/distractor content were preserved as activity actions and feedback; no conceptual error required correction, only boundary-scoping of the fossil-formation correction.
No comparative-efficacy or necessity claims (e.g. 'only doing teaches this', 'a static image cannot teach') are asserted; legacy framing was softened to scoped scaffold/limit statements.

probeDeeper: If you poured sand, then mud, then gravel into a jar, which ends up at the bottom — and which was poured first?
What does finding a sea creature's fossil in a cliff high on a hill tell you about that place long ago?
Someone says the higher fossil must be older because it's had longer up there. What's wrong with that?
assess.correctAnswer: The trilobite, in the lower layer, lived earlier: rock layers build up over time with the oldest at the bottom and the youngest on top, so a fossil in a lower layer was buried longer ago.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'the top layer is the oldest — it's been sitting there longest' (inverted superposition)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build layers by dropping sediment — each new layer lands ON TOP, so the bottom formed first; oldest at the bottom, youngest at the top.
errorPatterns.distractor: The ammonite — the top layer is the oldest because it has been there longest.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: picks the higher fossil (ammonite) as the earlier animal

errorPatterns.pattern: 'all the layers and fossils formed at the same time (one flood)' (single-event, no deep time)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Layers accumulate slowly, one atop another, over long stretches of time — different layers record different times.
errorPatterns.distractor: They lived at the same time — all the layers formed together.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: says both animals lived at the same time

errorPatterns.pattern: 'the fossil is the animal's actual body/bones, still there unchanged' (fossil = preserved remains, not mineralised)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach how fossils form: the remains are gradually replaced by minerals and turned to rock over long time.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: talks about the real bones or skin still being present in the rock

responseLevels.gap: Inverts superposition (top = oldest) or says all fossils/layers are the same age.
responseLevels.full: Applies superposition to order the fossils, reads fossils as evidence of different organisms at different times, and infers landscape change over long time (e.g. a sea fossil high on land = once underwater); transfers to a new cliff.
responseLevels.partial: Knows oldest-at-the-bottom for layers but doesn't connect a fossil's position to WHEN the organism lived, or can't read landscape change from it.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In a cliff face you find a trilobite fossil in a low layer and an ammonite fossil in a higher layer. Which animal lived earlier — and how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with inverted superposition picks the higher (ammonite) as older, reasoning 'it's been up there longest.' A child who imagines all layers forming together says they lived at the same time. Correct reasoning uses oldest-at-bottom AND reads fossil position as a record of time. The why-tier exposes which rule the child is using.
